To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) causal orientation is {\bf not} statistically decidable in LiNGAM models with latent confounders; and (2) that result holds for {\bf any} method that converges to the correct orientation in the limit.

(1) in the LiNGAM setting, causal relationships are identified and causal orientation is {\bf statistically decidable} when no latent confoundders are present, and that (2) in the LiNAGAM setting, causal orientation is {\it not} statistically decidable when latent confounders {\bf are} present, even if faithfullness is satisfied

(1) causal relationships in acyclic, linear causal models with latent confounders and non-Gaussian noise are not statistically decidable from observational data; (2) causal relationships in LiNGAM models with latent confounder and non-Gaussianity are not statistically decodable from observational data; and (3) causal orientation in LiNGAM causal models with latent variables and non-Gaussian errors is statistically decidable, but the probability of error converges to zero as sample size increases.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: \begin{itemize} \item How does statistical undecidability arise in the LiNGAM setting? \item Can we identify the conditions under which statistical undecidabilty arises? \item Can statistical undecidabiliy be avoided?

the following questions. \begin{itemize} \item What is the relationship between faithfulness and statistical decidability of causal orientation? \item What is required to restore decidability in the presence of confounders? \item What are the implications of statistical undecidability in causal inference?
the following question: what is the effect of the presence of latent variables on statistical decidability in linear, non-Gaussian models?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

causal orientation in LiNGAM models is not statistically decidable in the presence of unobserved confounders, but it is possible to adjust the model to achieve statistical decidability in the presence of confounders.

, if causal relationships are linear, non-Gaussian, and acyclic and faithfulness is satisfied, then causal orientation among observed and latent variables is identified, but not statistically decidable, and there are a number of possible adjustments that may recover statistical decidability.
, in the presence of a latent confounder, the LiNGAM causal orientation problem is not decidable, but the LiNGAM {\em model} may be identifiable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the presence of confounders, causal orientation among the observed variables is statistically undecidable, even if faith\-fulness is satisfied, but it can be made statistically decidable by adjusting the model to include a latent confounder for every pair of observed variables.

, in the presence of unmodeled latent confounders: (1) causal orientation among observed confounded variables is not statistically decidable, (2) causal orientation among unconfounded variables remains statistically decidable, and (3) causal orientation among all variables is statistically decidable in some modified LiNGAM model.
, in the presence of confounders, the LiNGAM causal model is not statistically decidable.
The main takeaway from our work is that

statistical decidability of causal orientation in linear, non-Gaussian causal models is sensitive to the assumptions made on the causal graph, and that the presence of latent variables is a particularly problematic assumption.
the presence of latent variables can be a serious obstacle to causal discovery.

the LiNGAM assumption of non-Gaussian noise terms is a very powerful one: it allows us to make strong inferences about causal relationships, even in the presence of unobserved confounders, when the causal model is acyclic.
